lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture this. You write a Blender add-on that needs NumPy, you type pip install, and Blender still says it has never heard of the module. What's going on?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'd have blamed pip. What's the real reason?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Blender ships its own Python. The pip on your system installs for a completely different interpreter. So Antoine wrote a small installer that talks to Blender's own Python instead.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does it find the right one?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Inside Blender, the system executable value points at Blender's bundled interpreter. The script runs pip through that, so packages are installed for the Python that will actually import them. It works on Windows with Blender 4.2 and up.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where do the packages go?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Into a per-user modules folder that Blender itself can name. It's writable without admin rights, and it survives add-on reloads. Then the script adds that folder to the import path, so the next import just works.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Think of it as a delivery driver who always uses the building's own side door rather than the front desk of a different building.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nice. What about waiting for downloads? Doesn't Blender freeze?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's the other trick. The install runs in a background thread, with a progress bar, so the interface stays responsive. Blender only lets the main thread touch the UI, so popups go through a timer that runs on the main side. You get a message when everything is installed.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Does it reinstall everything each time?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: No. It tries to import each package first and skips the ones already there, so a second run is quick. The list lives in one dictionary at the top, with pinned versions like meshio and requests.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Two ways. Paste it into the Scripting workspace, press Run Script and wait for the popup. Or call it from the add-on's register function, so the dependencies arrive with the add-on and users never have to guess which Python to use.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That sounds like fewer support emails.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Exactly. You own the package list in one place. The full write-up has the complete script and a screenshot of the Scripting workspace, if you want to copy it.
